strengths: Holistic multi-teacher formulation: The paper proposes an effective paradigm that distills complementary signals (language-aligned via SigLIP2, generalist visual features via DINOv3, and object/spatial awareness via PE-Spatial) into a shared 3DGS backbone, bridging high-level semantics and fine-grained spatial structure.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The proposed method is thoroughly benchmarked across diverse tasks (open-vocabulary semantic and instance segmentation, linear/decoder probing, full finetuning, and 3D VQA) on ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, and InteriorGS, consistently outperforming strong baselines like SceneSplat and Sonata.

High data and storage efficiency: Chorus achieves state-of-the-art results using significantly fewer pretraining scenes (up to 39.9x fewer than competitive point cloud SSL baselines). The proposed online render-and-distill adaptation strategy further circumvents the need for multi-terabyte offline pseudo-label feature storage.

Strong cross-modality transferability: When adapted as a point-cloud encoder (using only centers, colors, and normals), Chorus transfers remarkably well to point cloud benchmarks, supported by meaningful analyses on noise robustness and instance retrieval.

Insightful ablations: The ablation studies clearly dissect the role of each teacher, the impact of staged training (e.g., delaying PE-Spatial introduction), the contribution of 3DGS-aware augmentations, and feature standardization via PHI-S.
weaknesses: Omission of mathematical details for augmentations: While the conceptual motivation behind the Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold augmentations is convincing, the actual mathematical formulations are deferred to the supplementary material, making Section 3.4 less self-contained.

Training and architectural complexity: Staged training schedules, multiple projection heads, and combinations of matching and contrastive regularizers introduce additional system complexity compared to single-objective self-supervised approaches, though this is somewhat eased by PHI-S loss balancing.

Model size and inference overhead: As reported in Table 10, Chorus has a larger parameter footprint (131.3M) and slightly slower per-scene inference (0.70s) compared to SceneSplat (91.7M / 0.65s) and Sonata (108.5M / 0.49s).

strengths: Well-motivated holistic representation learning framework: Rather than relying on a single distillation target, the paper thoughtfully integrates complementary 2D foundation models (SigLIP2 for open-vocabulary language alignment, DINOv3 for generalist representations, and PE-Spatial for localized object cues) into a single 3DGS scene encoder.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Chorus is rigorously evaluated across diverse benchmarks and tasks, including zero-shot semantic segmentation, open-vocabulary instance segmentation, 3D VQA (via GaussianVLM), and linear/decoder probing and fine-tuning on both 3DGS and point cloud formats.

Cross-modality transfer and data efficiency: The point-cloud-compatible variant of Chorus demonstrates impressive transferability, outperforming or matching dedicated point cloud SSL methods (e.g., Sonata) while utilizing significantly fewer training scenes.

Practical render-and-distill adaptation: The proposed online rendering-based adaptation effectively leverages the native rendering capabilities of 3DGS, bypassing the substantial storage and I/O bottlenecks associated with precomputing dense 3D pseudo-labels for new domains.

3DGS-tailored design: The paper addresses the unique optimization dynamics of 3DGS through domain-specific augmentations (rendering-equivalent and immature-manifold perturbations) and feature standardization (PHI-S).
weaknesses: Omission of critical mathematical formulations in the main text: Key definitions, including the exact formulas for the 3DGS-aware augmentations and the instance/semantic contrastive regularizers, are relegated to the supplementary material, hindering standalone technical reproducibility.

Computational footprint and inference overhead: As reported in Table 10, Chorus incurs higher parameter count (131.3M) and slower inference time (0.70s/scene) compared to baselines like Sonata (108.5M, 0.49s) and SceneSplat (91.7M, 0.65s). A brief discussion on parameter/speed-accuracy trade-offs or model pruning would strengthen the work.

Pretraining offline overhead: While the rendering-based adaptation addresses downstream adaptation costs, the primary pretraining still depends on precomputing and uplifting multi-teacher features over large datasets, which demands considerable compute and engineering complexity.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a wide spectrum of downstream tasks, including zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic and instance segmentation, 3D visual question answering, linear/decoder probing, and data-efficient finetuning.

The proposed render-and-distill adaptation scheme effectively eliminates the heavy storage and I/O overhead associated with precomputing and storing gigabytes/terabytes of dense 3D pseudo-labels on novel scenes.

Interesting cross-modal transfer study demonstrating that an encoder pretrained on 3DGS parameters (centers, colors, normals) generalizes competitive feature representations to point-cloud benchmarks with notable data efficiency compared to self-supervised point cloud baselines.
Extensive ablations isolating the contribution of individual teachers (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial), loss terms, staged training, and rendering resolution.
weaknesses: The core conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental, as the overall pipeline primarily combines established paradigms: the 'lift-then-align' framework from SceneSplat, 2D multi-teacher agglomeration principles (similar to RADIO / AM-RADIO), PHI-S feature standardization, and the backbone architecture from Sonata.

Several key technical formulations lack explicit definition in the main text and are deferred to the supplementary material, notably the exact equations for the contrastive regularizers (Eq. 6) and the mathematical formulation of the two proposed 3DGS-aware augmentations (Sec. 3.4).

It is unclear how much of the performance advantage stems from the proposed framework itself versus the sheer scale and strength of the state-of-the-art 2D teacher models used (e.g., SigLIP2-so400m, DINOv3-ViT-L, PE-Spatial-L14) compared to baselines trained against older or smaller teachers.

Evaluation is exclusively restricted to indoor reconstructed environments (ScanNet, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, InteriorGS); applicability to large-scale unbounded outdoor environments or complex dynamic/sparse scenes remains unverified.

strengths: A well-motivated and versatile framework: Chorus tackles representation learning directly on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations by distilling complementary priors from diverse 2D foundation models (SigLIP2 for language alignment, DINOv3 for generalist visual features, and PE-Spatial for object-level awareness).

Novel 3DGS-specific augmentations: The proposed rendering-equivalent perturbation (grounded via second-order Taylor expansion) and immature-manifold perturbation account for the unique parameter dynamics of 3DGS, providing a principled alternative to naive point-cloud augmentations.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across a wide variety of tasks—including zero-shot open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, 3D VQA / reasoning with LLMs, and linear/decoder probing—demonstrating consistent and noticeable improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods like SceneSplat and Sonata.

Impressive cross-modality transfer and data efficiency: The point-cloud-compatible variant pretrained on Gaussian centers, colors, and normals outperforms strong SSL point cloud baselines on several benchmarks while using up to 39.9× fewer training scenes.
Practical render-and-distill adaptation strategy: An online rendering-based adaptation scheme eliminates the need for expensive 3D pseudo-label preprocessing when adapting to novel scenes/domains.
weaknesses: High precomputation and training overhead: Although the render-and-distill adaptation helps for novel domains, initial multi-teacher pretraining requires extracting dense feature maps from multiple heavy 2D foundation models (e.g., SigLIP2-so400m, DINOv3-ViT-L) and uplifting them to 3DGS across thousands of scenes, which involves notable storage and computation.

Parameter count and inference runtime: As shown in Table 12, Chorus has a larger parameter footprint (131.3M) and higher inference latency (0.70s/scene) compared to baselines like SceneSplat (91.7M, 0.65s) and Sonata (108.5M, 0.49s).

Architectural specificity for 3DGS input features: The main paper briefly states adapting the 5-stage transformer from Sonata, but could provide clearer exposition in the main text regarding how non-geometric splat attributes (quaternions, scales, opacities) are embedded into the initial transformer stages compared to the point-cloud variant.

strengths: Well-motivated multi-teacher pretraining framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene encoding, effectively harmonizing complementary representations (SigLIP2 for language semantics, DINOv3 for general visual structure, and PE-Spatial for object-level spatial locality) via a shared backbone and dedicated projection heads.

Technically sound, domain-specific designs including 3DGS-aware augmentations (rendering-equivalent position noise and immature-manifold scale inflation) that are mathematically justified via second-order Taylor expansion and empirically validated against standard point-cloud jittering.

The lightweight render-and-distill adaptation strategy provides a practical solution to avoid the massive offline storage and preprocessing overhead typically required for dense 3D pseudo-label generation during domain transfer.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across a diverse range of tasks: open-vocabulary semantic/instance segmentation, 3D VQA integration (GaussianVLM), linear/decoder probing, and data-efficient supervision benchmarks.

Strong empirical results and transferability; the model outperforms existing 3DGS baselines (SceneSplat) and demonstrates surprising competitiveness on point-cloud benchmarks compared to specialized point-cloud self-supervised baselines (Sonata) with substantially fewer pretraining scenes.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: multi-teacher distillation from 2D vision foundation models and 'lift-then-align' frameworks are established paradigms in 2D (RADIO, PHI-S) and 3D (SceneSplat, LUDVIG), meaning the core conceptual leap lies primarily in unifying and tailoring these components to 3DGS.

The base pretraining stage still depends heavily on offline 2D feature extraction and 3D uplifting across thousands of scenes; the render-and-distill mechanism is currently evaluated primarily for adaptation rather than end-to-end pretraining from scratch.
Increased model complexity and compute: Table 12 shows that Chorus requires 131.3M parameters and is slower at inference (0.70s per scene) than SceneSplat (91.7M / 0.65s) and Sonata (108.5M / 0.49s).

The cross-modality point-cloud evaluation is not direct cross-modal inference of the native 3DGS checkpoint; rather, it requires pretraining a separate point-cloud-compatible variant that takes only coordinates, colors, and estimated normals as inputs.

strengths: Holistic and well-motivated framework: Extending multi-teacher knowledge distillation from 2D vision foundation models (SigLIP2, DINOv3, PE-Spatial) into a unified, feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) encoder is a timely, principled, and impactful direction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The submission benchmarks across a wide variety of tasks and settings, including zero-shot semantic and instance segmentation, linear/decoder probing, data-efficient supervision regimes, cross-modal transfer to point clouds, and LLM-based 3D visual question answering (GaussianVLM integration).

Tailored 3DGS design components: The introduction of 3DGS-aware augmentations (Rendering-Equivalent and Immature-Manifold perturbations) addresses the core optimization dynamics and rendering characteristics of 3D Gaussians rather than naively applying point-cloud jitter.

Practical out-of-domain adaptation: The proposed online render-and-distill adaptation pipeline provides an effective mechanism to adapt pretrained 3DGS encoders to novel scenes without requiring costly offline 3D pseudo-label lifting or heavy disk storage overhead.

Remarkable data efficiency and transfer: Demonstrating that a point-cloud-compatible variant of Chorus matches or exceeds self-supervised point cloud baselines like Sonata while using ~40x fewer pretraining scenes is a strong and insightful finding.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is primarily an integration of established paradigms: While adapting multi-teacher distillation (e.g., RADIO, DUNE) and 'lift-then-align' frameworks (e.g., SceneSplat) to 3DGS is very well-engineered and executed, the high-level methodology is a natural combination of these existing ideas.

Pretraining storage and compute overhead: Although the render-and-distill recipe simplifies adaptation, initial pretraining still relies heavily on precomputing and lifting high-dimensional 2D features (over 1 TB of storage noted for InteriorGS alone), which remains a hurdle for scaling up.

Mixed performance in specific point-cloud probing setups: For instance, in Table 6 under linear probing on ScanNet Val instance segmentation, Sonata notably outperforms Chorus (72.6 vs. 66.6 mAP25), indicating that distillation over 3DGS does not uniformly dominate self-supervised geometric pretraining in all single-scene instance settings.
